title: Tanween: the hidden 'n' at the end

bigIdea.text: A doubled vowel mark on the last letter adds an 'n' sound: '-an', '-un' or '-in'. You hear the n, but it is not written as a letter.

proper.text: Tanween fath ( ً ): two fathas, '-an'. Tanween damm ( ٌ ): two dammas (often drawn as a damma with a small tail), '-un'. Tanween kasr ( ٍ ): two kasras below, '-in'.
Tanween only comes on the last letter of a word. It is an extra n sound (a noon with sukun) that is pronounced but not written.
Tanween fath usually has an alif after it (ـًا). When you continue, that alif is not read: say '-an'. When you stop on the word, drop the n and say a long 'aa' (2 counts).
When you stop on tanween damm or tanween kasr, drop both the vowel and the n: end on the letter with sukun.
Before some letters the n of tanween hides or merges into the next word; Stage 2 covers this. Before a hamza, as in the examples below, it stays a clear 'n'.

extras.text: In printed Madinah mushafs the two marks are drawn stacked when the n is said clearly, and staggered (one slightly after the other) when it hides or merges into the next letter. This app's text does not show that difference, so listen to Sheikh al-Minshawi.

note.text: Tanween fath with its alif: '-an' when you continue (here a hamza follows, so the n is clear).
Tanween kasr on the first word: a clear '-in' before the hamza of the next word.
The same pattern: tanween kasr, then a word starting with hamza.
Tanween damm at the end of the ayah: when you stop, drop '-un' and end on د with sukun.
Tanween kasr at the end of the ayah: stopping, you end on ر with sukun.

drills.prompt: Say بً بٌ بٍ (ban, bun, bin), then تً تٌ تٍ.
Stopping practice: say بَتًا as 'batan' (continuing), then as 'bataa' (stopping). Say بَتٌ as 'batun', then 'bat'.

tip.text: بُ is 'bu'. بٌ is 'bun': the doubled damma adds an n.

explain: Tanween is an n sound (it only turns into m in a special case, Stage 2).
A long 'aa' comes from fatha + alif, or from stopping on tanween fath.
Tanween is a sound, not a pause.
'bi' is a single kasra, without the n.

options: Only on the last letter of a word
On the first letter of a word
explain: It is always at the end.
It sits on the last letter, whatever that letter is.

questions.q: Tanween fath often has an alif after it (ـًا). Is that alif read when you continue?
options: Yes: say a long 'aa' and then 'n'
Yes: it turns the tanween into '-in'
explain: Right: the alif only matters when you stop.
That adds a long vowel that isn't there when continuing.

questions.q: You stop on a word ending in tanween fath with alif (ـًا). How do you finish?
explain: The n is dropped when you stop.
When stopping it becomes long, not short.
The vowel stays; it is the n that drops.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT tanween?

explain: A single damma gives 'u' without the n.

questions.q: You stop on a word ending in tanween damm (ـٌ). How do you finish?
options: Drop the '-un' and end on the letter with sukun
explain: The vowel and the n drop when you stop.
There is no long vowel here.
The vowel is not changed to 'a'.

questions.q: Why is tanween called a 'hidden n'?
options: It is pronounced but not written as a ن letter
It is written as a small ن
explain: You do pronounce it when you continue.
It is written as doubled vowel marks, not as a ن.
It appears on many kinds of words.

questions.q: How do you read بً when you continue to the next word?
explain: 'baa' is how you stop on ـًا, not how you continue.

questions.q: Which pair differs only by tanween?
Tanween is really which sound added at the end of a word?
explain: It is an n, not an m.
A long alif only appears when you stop on tanween fath.

questions.q: You stop on a word with tanween kasr (ـٍ). What do you say at the end?
options: Just the letter with sukun: no '-in'
explain: The vowel and the n drop when you stop.
There is no long vowel here.
The vowel is not changed to 'a'.

remnote: Tanween ( ً ٌ ٍ ) == Doubled vowel mark on the last letter: -an, -un, -in (a hidden n)
Tanween fath + alif (ـًا) when continuing == Say '-an'; the alif is not read
Stopping on tanween fath (ـًا) == Say a long 'aa' (2 counts), no n
Stopping on tanween damm or kasr == Drop the vowel and the n; end with sukun
